newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian demand rescues gold price - HK exchange head.
newsitem.headline: Asian demand rescues gold price - HK exchange head.

text.p: Heavy gold buying by Asian end-users, such as jewellery manufacturers, as the precious metal slid to recent 3-1/4-year lows has now propped up prices preventing a freefall, the head of Hong Kong's gold market said.

Spot gold opened at $354.10/$354.60 an ounce in Hong Kong on Wednesday, little changed from New York's overnight firmer close, but sharply above the lows around $336 hit on February 12, which were a new nadir for the metal since April, 1993.

"If the physical (gold) didn't prop that demand in Asia, probably (the price) would be around $330 today," Raymond Chan Fat-chu, head of Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society told Reuters in a recent interview.
Chan said Hong Kong had imported between 35-38 tonnes of gold in January and so far in February, compared with 20 tonnes over this period in a more average year.

He said the dip in the gold price into the $330-$340 range had probably sparked the purchase of an additional 13-15 tonnes of gold in Hong Kong, combined with a further 2-3 tones from a pick-up in buying for the Chinese New Year holiday period.
"The price between $330 and $340 triggered the buying on the streets, and when the street buyers take the physical I have to go looking to London or elsewhere to buy," Chan said.
He said after the rollercoaster ride in prices during the early part of 1997 he now expected gold prices to be more volatile for the remainder of the year than they were in 1996.

Hong Kong's imports of gold in unwrought, semi-manufactured or powder form and of gold coins fell to 208.18 tonnes in 1996 from about 259 tonnes in 1995, Hong Kong Census and Statistics Departments released on Tuesday showed.
